title: Reliability Under Randomness: An Empirical Analysis of Sparse and Dense Language Model Behavior Across Decoding Temperatures
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models become less reliable than dense language models when decoding temperature increases and generation becomes more stochastic. The core research question is whether conditional computation in sparse architectures interacts with temperature-based sampling in ways that reduce output stability, accuracy, and compliance on deterministic tasks.

To study this, the author evaluates three large language models—OLMoE-7B (sparse base model), Mixtral-8x7B (sparse instruction-tuned model), and Qwen2.5-3B (dense instruction-tuned model)—on two deterministic reasoning tasks: variable binding and multi-step arithmetic. The study compares model behavior across four decoding settings (greedy, T=0.1, T=0.5, and T=1.0) and analyzes accuracy, format compliance, consistency across repeated generations, confidence, and failure modes. The dataset consists of benchmark-like prompt-response generations rather than human participants or educational users.

There is no K-12, school, literacy, or foundational reading population in this paper. The work is a technical model-behavior evaluation conducted on arithmetic reasoning tasks in a computational setting using an NVIDIA A100 GPU. It does not test any educational intervention, classroom implementation, tutoring system, reading support tool, or generative AI application for phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or reading comprehension.

The main conclusion is that instruction tuning, not sparse versus dense architecture, is the primary factor associated with robustness to temperature-induced randomness. The sparse instruction-tuned model (Mixtral) remained stable across temperatures similarly to the dense instruction-tuned model (Qwen), whereas the sparse base model (OLMoE) degraded as temperature increased. For the targeted evidence question, this paper is a clear negative finding / non-relevant near-miss: it provides no direct causal or quasi-experimental evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes using generative AI, and should not be counted as evidence for literacy intervention effectiveness.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an arXiv technical benchmark paper on language model decoding reliability, not a K-12 education intervention study. It includes no classroom, school-supported, or learner sample; no randomized or quasi-experimental design relevant to educational outcomes; and no direct foundational reading measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no K-12 literacy or foundational reading impact, and therefore provides no causal evidence for generative AI effects on phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or reading comprehension. It is a clear negative match for the targeted evidence search, serving only as an adjacent technical near-miss rather than education evidence.
